extracted.intended_audience: Choice of Games authors, ChoiceScript interactive-fiction writers, and narrative/game writers interested in commercial IF workflow
extracted.subtask_short: writing Choice of Games interactive fiction
extracted.subtask_description: A practical, project-level workflow for planning, coding, drafting, testing, and revising Choice of Games / ChoiceScript interactive-fiction projects, aimed at producing publishable commercial IF. Focuses on how to structure concepting, chapter outlines, coding-as-outlining, playtesting, and editorial rounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concept / elevator pitch
rubrics_metrics.description: Build an elevator-pitch paragraph to send to your editor that includes the PC's role, the choices they're facing, a few different ways in which they might handle problems, some overarching goals, and a few major NPCs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start from an idea/vibes/general sense of the game (often something that's been 'rattling around' for a while). The elevator pitch distills the seed into a concise paragraph for editorial consideration (examples: Creme de la Creme idea sprung from Blood Money work; The Earth Has Teeth idea was seeded years before).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chapter-by-chapter outline
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop the concept into a chapter-by-chapter outline that includes the PC's stats, mutually-exclusive goals, NPC relationships, major branches, and how the PC is engaging with the world at each stage of the game.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a choice per chapter to show how the mechanics will work. Expect at least one revision in response to your editor's thoughts (author gives examples: asked to include more concrete PC goals or specify why a PC is assigned a role). Tweak stats at this stage; author notes they 'tend to err on the side of more complexity and then realise... streamlining would be wise.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Chapter planning: scene-by-scene, know endings and branches
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan chapters by hand with a broad-strokes scene-by-scene outline, knowing how and where the chapter will end, in what ways it will be branched at that ending, and what is required from the chapter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For shorter chapters or when precision with stats is required, plan individual choices (example: Noblesse Oblige work to a tight wordcount). Ensure awareness of where branches are and plan so branches are evenly spread and you have a sense of what every character is up to (example: Chapter 3 of Honor Bound planning to evenly distribute character time during a camping trip).

rubrics_metrics.name: Code-as-outlining: code whole chapters before drafting
rubrics_metrics.description: Code the whole of a chapter (sometimes two) before drafting prose to use coding as a way of doing further planning and understanding chapter size/complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coding at this stage makes the content playable and testable; it's where many interactions and playable ideas emerge. The author prefers separating coding creativity (mechanics/interaction design) from drafting creativity (prose). Some writers draft and code simultaneously, but coding-first gives better planning clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make code playable and test stats thoroughly
rubrics_metrics.description: Include all stat changes and stat tests when coding so chapters are playable and testable either manually or using ChoiceScript testing tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ChoiceScript's QuickTest and RandomTest features. Use a variation of 'Emily Short's method' to test how difficult stat tests are. Use RandomTest to check how many times a stat is tested on average and tweak if one stat is disproportionately powerful compared to another. Anti-pattern: rushing to drafting without checking stats leads to regrets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage stats complexity and balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Design and revise stats intentionally: start with more complexity if needed, then streamline; monitor and rebalance so no stat is disproportionately powerful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tweak stats as part of outline revisions or after coding/testing. The author explicitly notes they 'err on the side of more complexity and then realise... that streamlining would be wise.' Use testing feedback (RandomTest, playtests) to identify imbalance and adjust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting tied to code skeleton, not raw wordcount
rubrics_metrics.description: Set drafting targets based on progress through your code skeleton (how far through the code you are) rather than raw daily/weekly wordcount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This metric gives a better sense of scope and is less demoralising on low-wordcount/high-productivity days. The author usually works top-to-bottom of the text file but sometimes starts with the end or complicated, repetitive, or wordy scenes (e.g., intimate scenes or repeated date/proposal scenes). After drafting a chapter, playtest it and revise before sending it to your editor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative revising and editorial responsiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: When you receive editor notes, repeat the cycle of chapter planning, coding, drafting, and revising; incorporate WIP-sharing and player feedback during development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect multiple revision passes. The outline will go through at least one revision in response to editorial feedback, and later stages will involve intensive triage and prioritisation of feedback. Be willing to add substantial new writing during revisions (author notes adding 'tens of thousands of words' during these stages).

rubrics_metrics.name: Review, playtesting, continuity reading, and feedback triage
rubrics_metrics.description: Before finalising, have a fresh Choice of Games editor play the full game, invite external testers, and employ continuity readers to spot errors or confusing text; then triage and prioritise feedback for revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This stage is intense: requires feedback triage, prioritisation, attention to detail, and humility. Make changes in response to tester/editor/continuity feedback; afterwards the game goes to CoG's copyeditor. Typical timeframe from sending to copyeditor to release is two to three months.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workflow rhythm and project timeline
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow a repeating pipeline: concept → outline → chapter planning → coding → drafting → revising → review/playtesting → copyediting → release; start new elevator pitches during mid-to-late stages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes this loop is cyclical and that they often begin thinking of new ideas during playtesting or late-stage drafting. Timeframes vary by game size and copyeditor availability; expect months of work and potential significant additions during playtesting/revision.
